caption:
What kind of dark circles do I have?
Probably more than one kind, and they do not respond to the same things.

Dark circles are not one condition. Some are pigment in the skin itself - a brown band that often runs in families. Some are vessels showing through thin skin, which reads blue or purple. Some are shadow, cast by the shape of the area rather than by any colour at all. And some are colour left behind by rubbing, allergies or eczema.

At a skin clinic in Singapore, dermatologists examined 200 patients with dark circles. The vessel type was the most common overall (41.8%), mostly in Chinese patients; the pigment type was the most common in Indian and Malay patients. Many people had more than one type, which is why the numbers add up to more than 100.

Two checks you can do at a mirror. Gently stretch the skin under the eye: if it lightens, structure is part of it; if it darkens or turns bluer, vessels are; if nothing changes, it is likely pigment. Then tilt your chin up toward a window: darkness that fades in direct light is shadow.

This is a hint, not a diagnosis, and it comes from patients who chose to see a dermatologist rather than the general population. One more thing worth knowing: in an Indian clinic study, half the patients with dark circles were also anaemic. Anaemia is common there anyway, so that is not proof of cause - but darkness that is new, alongside tiredness, is worth mentioning to a doctor.

Ranu H et al. Dermatol Surg 2011. doi:10.1111/j.1524-4725.2011.02065.x
Sheth PB et al. Indian J Dermatol 2014. doi:10.4103/0019-5154.127675
